summary: A Healthline article on using tea tree oil (from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves) on hair, covering benefits for dandruff and hair health, research on hirsutism and a 5% tea tree shampoo dandruff study, usage instructions, and risks such as toxicity if ingested and skin irritation. It concludes that tea tree oil can be an effective dandruff remedy, that patch testing is advised, and that people with allergies or who are pregnant or breastfeeding should be careful. Navigation and footer boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: Healthline overview of tea tree oil for hair, covering dandruff and hair-health benefits, supporting studies, usage methods, and safety precautions.
key_facts: Tea tree oil is derived from the leaves of the Melaleuca alternifolia plant.
The article states tea tree oil likely won't help hair loss caused by autoimmune conditions, chemotherapy, genetic predisposition, or aging.
Dandruff is caused by an accumulation of scaly, dry skin on the scalp.
A shampoo containing tea tree oil can provide both antifungal and antibacterial benefits for the scalp.
A study in the Journal of Endocrinological Investigation gave women with hirsutism lavender and tea tree oil spray twice per day for three months, resulting in decreased hair diameter.
A study in the Journal of American Academy of Dermatology tested a shampoo with 5 percent tea tree oil on 126 participants over four weeks.
The 5 percent tea tree oil shampoo caused a 41 percent improvement in dandruff in that study.
For dandruff, the article recommends lathering a 5 percent tea tree oil shampoo for 3 minutes daily for 4 weeks.
For healthy hair, the article suggests diluting tea tree oil with almond oil or a similar oil at a 1 to 10 ratio, used every day.
Tea tree oil must not be ingested; ingestion can cause loss of muscle control and balance and can even lead to a coma.
Tea tree oil contains 1,8-cineole, which is known to irritate some people's skin.
Users should test products on the lower inside of the arm and wait 12 to 24 hours for a reaction before use.
People allergic to Balsam of Peru, benzoin, colophony tinctures, eucalyptol, or myrtle family plants have a greater probability of being allergic to tea tree oil.
Listed side effects include depression, diarrhea, drowsiness, fatigue, muscle tremors, itching, and rashes.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should talk to a doctor before using tea tree oil on their hair.
The article was medically reviewed by Debra Rose Wilson and written by Jennifer Purdie, updated April 12, 2017.
